title: VCP
teaches: The VCP (volatility contraction pattern) as we trade it: a leader in an uptrend pulls back in a run of swings that each get smaller, volume dries up into the tight final swing, the pivot is the high of that final swing, the buy is the trade through it at market in regular hours and no more than 4% past it, the stop sits a few cents under the entry day's low, the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, with the rest on the trail, and a loss at the stop is the system working.

facts.quote: Stop first (by default a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low, F62); the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.

facts.quote: Shares = account × risk % ÷ (entry − stop), rounded down, then capped: the size is the SMALLER of the risk-based size and the position cap

facts.claim: A5: the full size at one price with one stop; no adding.

facts.claim: A13: the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy.

facts.quote: The stop may move up to breakeven between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell.
facts.claim: Our stop may move up to breakeven between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell.

facts.quote: A gap against the stop: the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day decide. The low of the first 30-minute bar is the new stop.
facts.claim: B20: on a gap through the stop, the first 30-minute low is the new stop.

facts.quote: With a ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.
facts.claim: B20's ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.

facts.quote: No new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report; hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R.
facts.claim: B22: no new buys in the 3 days before a report; hold through one only if up 5R.

facts.quote: Trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day.
facts.claim: B23: only stocks at $10 or more trading at least $20 million a day.

facts.quote: The 200-day line: no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long; shorts only below the 200-day, never above it unless it is a parabolic short.
facts.claim: B26: no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, except a parabolic long.

facts.quote: No chasing: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.
facts.claim: C28: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.

facts.quote: Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink (A5).
facts.claim: C28: chasing costs size, because the stop stays put and the distance grows.

facts.quote: Too stretched to buy: skip a long that is more than 10% above its 9 EMA.
facts.claim: We skip a long that is more than 10% above its 9 EMA: too stretched to buy.

facts.quote: Buy leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups, except parabolic and mean-reversion trades.
facts.claim: C31: buy leaders, an RS rating of 80 or more in a strong group.

facts.quote: Time stop: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money.
facts.claim: C33: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold.

facts.quote: Never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume; illiquid stocks are not even watched.
facts.claim: D42: never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume.

facts.quote: Later sells are a judgment too: sell more into strength on a later push, and trail what is left.
facts.claim: Later sells are a judgment: sell more into strength on a later push, and trail what is left.

facts.quote: Default trail: the 9 EMA for fast movers, the 20 EMA for steadier ones; sell what is left on a close below it.
facts.claim: Our default trail: the 9 EMA for fast movers, the 20 EMA for steadier ones; a close below it sells what is left.

facts.quote: Entries are market orders.
facts.claim: E57: entries are market orders.

facts.quote: No new buys outside regular trading hours.
facts.claim: E58: no new buys outside regular hours.

facts.quote: The stop sits a few cents under the day's low, not exactly on it.
facts.claim: F62: the stop sits a few cents under the day's low.

facts.quote: The market reading as a guide (A10): Green, full risk per grade and up to 10 positions; Yellow, smaller and fewer; Orange, only A+ setups; Red, mostly cash and shorts.
facts.claim: F65: Green full risk; Yellow smaller and fewer; Orange only A+; Red mostly cash and shorts.

facts.quote: After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule.
facts.claim: B21: after a stop-out, buy again only on a new trigger, as a new trade.

facts.quote: In a Red market: mostly cash, plus shorts below the 200-day.
facts.claim: D46: in a Red market, mostly cash.

facts.quote: Never take a trade from an alert, a post or a video without your own entry, stop and size by these rules.
facts.claim: F66: never take a trade from an alert, a post or a video without your own entry, stop and size.

facts.quote: No setup, no trade: never force a trade to have something on; cash is a position.
facts.claim: D44: no setup, no trade; cash is a position.

facts.quote: Every planned buy has its entry, stop and size written down before the market opens.
facts.claim: D39: entry, stop and size written down before the open.

facts.quote: I want to see the stock move from greater volatility on the left side of the price base to lesser volatility on the right side.
facts.claim: Minervini: volatility should fall from the left side of the base to the right.

facts.quote: As a rule of thumb, I like to see each successive contraction contained to about half (plus or minus a reasonable amount) of the previous pullback or contraction.
facts.claim: Minervini: each contraction about half of the one before, give or take.

facts.quote: The progressive reduction in price volatility, which will be accompanied by a reduction in volume at particular points, eventually signifies that the base has been completed.
facts.claim: Minervini: shrinking swings and falling volume at points signal a finished base.

facts.quote: a flat base structure that is four to seven weeks in duration. With this type of base, there is no real volatility contraction as it remains a tight and narrow pattern or box
facts.claim: Minervini: a four-to-seven-week flat base is a box with no real volatility contraction.

facts.quote: from a 25 percent correction, to a 10 percent, to a 5 percent, and so forth, which would be indicative of a classic VCP progression.
facts.claim: Minervini: 25 percent, then 10, then 5 is a classic VCP progression.

facts.quote: I never go against the long-term trend. I look to go long a stage 2 uptrend and go short a stage 4 downtrend, plain and simple.
facts.claim: Minervini: long only in a Stage 2 uptrend.

facts.quote: If you're too late, you run the risk of buying a late-stage base that is obvious to everyone and prone to failure.
facts.claim: Minervini: a late-stage base is obvious to everyone and prone to failure.

facts.quote: To time my entry, I look for price consolidations, which are momentary pauses or periods of rest within the context of a prior uptrend.
facts.claim: Minervini: the consolidation is a pause inside a prior uptrend.

facts.quote: Lack of volume however, does raise a red flag; volume would need to come in soon after. As always, maintain your stop regardless.
facts.claim: Minervini: light breakout volume is a red flag; keep the stop regardless.

facts.quote: The pivot is the top of the final contraction. Not the highest price of the entire base, but the level the final tight consolidation keeps running into.
facts.claim: ChartMill: the pivot is the top of the final contraction, not the base's highest price.

facts.quote: The final contraction is the most important one. It has to be tight: ideally under 10%, and the closer to 3% to 6%, the better.
facts.claim: ChartMill: the final contraction must be tight, ideally under 10%, best 3% to 6%.

facts.quote: If you see several down days on heavy volume in the right half of the base, there is still distribution going on in the stock and you are too early.
facts.claim: ChartMill: several heavy down days in the right half mean distribution; you are too early.

facts.quote: A first or second base after the start of a new uptrend has better odds than a third or fourth.
facts.claim: ChartMill: a first or second base has better odds than a third or fourth.

facts.quote: In a negative market environment, even perfect VCPs fail en masse, simply because there aren't enough buyers to carry breakouts through.
facts.claim: ChartMill: in a negative market even perfect VCPs fail en masse.

facts.quote: An orderly pullback and consolidation with higher lows and tightening range in the consolidation phase.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: an orderly consolidation with higher lows and a tightening range.

facts.quote: The pivot is the high of the final contraction. It may sit below the base's left-side high.
facts.claim: The pivot is the high of the final contraction; it may sit below the base's high.

facts.quote: The first (deepest) contraction is 10% to 40%. Never a base that fell 60% or more.
facts.claim: The first contraction is 10% to 40%; never a base that fell 60% or more.

facts.quote: The final contraction is 10% or less; 3% to 6% with tight closes is best, 8% to 10% with loose closes is B-.
facts.claim: The final contraction is 10% or less; 3% to 6% with tight closes is best.

facts.quote: Higher lows: the final contraction's low is above the lowest low of the base.
facts.claim: The final contraction's low is above the base's lowest low.

facts.quote: Volume dries up: the final contraction's average daily volume is below the first contraction's and below the 50-day average, with at least one day in the final contraction at or under half the 50-day average.
facts.claim: Volume dries up into the final contraction.

facts.quote: No selling on the right side: no down day in the second half of the base on volume of 1.5 times the 50-day average or more.
facts.claim: No heavy down day in the second half of the base.

facts.quote: A grade cue: a pivot at or near a 52-week or all-time high (no overhead supply) is A+; a pivot well below the left-side high is B-.
facts.claim: A grade cue: a pivot near a 52-week or all-time high is A+.

facts.claim: A grade cue: a shakeout of a nearby low that recovers, then a higher low.

facts.claim: Three or four clean contractions, each about half the last, is the A+ picture.

facts.claim: A first contraction over 40%, or a fall of 60% or more, ends it.

facts.claim: A close below the final contraction's low restarts the count.

facts.claim: A heavy-volume down day in the right half ends it before the buy.

facts.claim: Price more than 4% above the pivot when you find it is a skip.

facts.quote: After the buy: a breakout day that closes back inside the base (the squat) is the warning with the worst numbers in the scan, not an exit by itself.

facts.claim: Warnings, not exits: a close under the 20-day soon after, three lower lows on rising volume.

facts.claim: Best as a first or second base; a third or fourth base late in a long run is a mistake.

facts.claim: One full buy at one price, one stop. No pilot buys, no adding.

walkthroughs.title: ON, August 2017: four pullbacks, each about half the last
steps: ON in 2017, a leader in an uptrend. It pulls back four times: 19.4%, 7.8%, 5.8%, then 3.5%. Each one smaller.
I like to see volume dry up into that last tight swing. Its high, 16.47, is the pivot.
August 30 it trades through 16.47 on 1.7 times volume. Buy at market. Stop just under the day's low, 15.85.
The worry is a close back inside the base. It held. 3R took 20 days, so this one takes patience.

walkthroughs.title: JOYY, January 2014: the pivot below the base high
steps: JOYY ran 146%, then built a six-week base. Three pullbacks, each smaller: 18.4%, 10.7%, then just 3.7%.
The base high on the left is 56.75. The last swing tops out lower, at 51.22. That's your pivot.
January 2, 2014, it clears 51.22 on 1.9 times volume. Buy at market, stop just under the day's low, 49.27.
Lose the day's low in the first few days and you're out. Instead, 3R the very next day, and you hold.

walkthroughs.title: ALGN, October 2007: the squat
steps: ALGN built a 59-session base in 2007 with two contractions, 27.5% then 7.1%. The pivot is 28.64.
October 17 it trades through on 2.3 times volume. Buy 28.65, stop 27.70, 3.3% away.
It closes at 28.14, back inside the base. A squat, the worst warning in our numbers. Not an exit by itself.
Next day it trades to 27.64 and takes the stop. Take the loss. A new buy needs a new trigger.

questions.q: What does a VCP stand for?
questions.why: Volatility Contraction Pattern. The name is about price swings that contract. A sideways wiggle whose contractions do not shrink is not a VCP.
questions.lesson_line: VCP stands for volatility contraction pattern. The swings in the base contract.

wrong.Volume Compression Pattern: Volume matters, but the name is about the size of the price swings.
wrong.Velocity Confirmation Pattern: That is not the name. A VCP is named for price swings that contract.
wrong.Volatile Continuation Pattern: The name says contraction, not continuation. It is named for swings that shrink.

questions.simple: The name is Volatility Contraction Pattern, as the price swings in the base contract more and more.

reasons: the name is quoted from the ChartMill guide; the Minervini archive pages could not be reopened in this pass

questions.q: The day before the breakout. Each pullback in this base is smaller than the one before it.
questions.why: True, and that's the whole idea. The first pullback is the deepest, then each one gets shallower. ON went 19.4%, then 7.8%, then 5.8%, then just 3.5%. Each dip meets fewer sellers, so it can't push price down as far. If the swings stop shrinking, I don't call it a VCP.
questions.lesson_line: Big swings on the left, small ones on the right. That's the shape we want.
questions.simple: True. Each dip meets fewer sellers, so each pullback is shallower than the last.

questions.why: Smaller. Each successive pullback in a VCP is smaller than the one before. A wiggle that does not shrink is not a VCP.
questions.lesson_line: Every pullback in a VCP is smaller than the last.

questions.q: Where's the pivot on this base, the price you buy through?
choices: The top of the last, tight swing
The highest price in the whole base
The low of the first pullback
questions.answer: The top of the last, tight swing
questions.why: The top of the last, tight swing. On JOYY that's 51.22. The base high on the left, 56.75, sits higher, and that's fine. The last swing is where sellers kept turning it back, so that's the line to clear. Mark it the night before and set an alert. When it trades through 51.22, you buy at market.
questions.lesson_line: The pivot is the top of the last tight swing, not always the base high.

wrong.The low of the first pullback: That's the bottom of the deepest dip, nowhere near where buyers prove themselves.
wrong.The highest price in the whole base: Waiting for the old high means buying well after the real breakout. The pivot can sit under the base high.
wrong.Yesterday's closing price: One close isn't a level. The pivot comes from the base, the high of that last swing.

questions.simple: The pivot is the top of the last, tight swing. Price through it means the last sellers are used up.

reasons: the pivot is a proposed card criterion, not an owner ruling

questions.story: A leader rested six weeks after a big run. Three pullbacks, each one smaller. It may break out tomorrow.

questions.q: A VCP's pivot may sit below the highest high of the base.
questions.why: True. The pivot is the high of the final contraction, and it may sit below the base's left-side high. ChartMill says the same: it is not the highest price of the entire base. A pivot well below the left-side high does grade B-, so it is a weaker location, but it is still the pivot.
questions.lesson_line: The pivot is the last swing's high, even when the base high is higher.
questions.simple: True, because the pivot is the high of the last swing, and that can sit below the highest price in the base.

reasons: pivot and its grade cue are proposed card criteria

questions.q: The VCP trades through its pivot during regular hours. You buy it with a market order, right there.
questions.why: True. Our entries are market orders. Price goes through the pivot, you hit it and you're in. A limit order can sit there unfilled while the stock runs away. Then you're chasing, and past 4% over the pivot it's a pass anyway. No new buys before the open or after the close either. Regular hours only.
questions.lesson_line: Through the pivot, regular hours, market order. That's the buy.
questions.simple: True. A market order gets you in as it breaks, and a resting limit can miss the move.

deeper.counter: Some guides tell you to rest a buy stop-limit order just above the pivot. We don't. Our entries are market orders, placed in regular hours as price trades through the pivot.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (E57 market orders, E58 regular hours)

questions.q: Where does your stop go?
choices: A few cents under today's low
In your head, no order yet
questions.answer: A few cents under today's low
questions.why: A few cents under today's low. The low of the day, LOD, is where this breakout is wrong. If price trades back through it, the buyers who pushed it through the pivot are gone. Go a few cents under, not right on it, so a tick to the low doesn't take you out. Then size from that stop. On ALGN that put the stop at 27.70 on a 28.65 buy. The base's low works too, it's just further away.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, a few cents under the low of the day. Size comes second.

wrong.Right on today's low: Right on the low gets tagged by a normal retest. A few cents under gives it that tick.
wrong.Wherever it fits your size: That's backwards. The stop comes from the chart, then the size comes from the stop.
wrong.In your head, no order yet: A stop in your head sells nothing. It goes in as a real order with the broker.

questions.simple: A few cents under today's low. That's where the breakout is wrong, and your size comes from it.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, F62) and the held decision D-008 on which low

questions.story: You bought this breakout today as it traded through the pivot. Today's bar is the last one on the chart.

questions.q: This stock sits under a falling 200-day, but its base is tight with shrinking swings. It's a VCP we can buy.
questions.why: False. A VCP is a leader resting inside an uptrend. Under a falling 200-day the stock is still in a downtrend. A tight range there is just a pause on the way down. Below the 200-day we don't buy stocks. That's a hard line, however tight the base looks.
questions.lesson_line: No uptrend, no VCP. Under the 200-day we don't buy stocks.
questions.simple: False. Under the 200-day the stock is in a downtrend, and we don't buy stocks there, however tight it looks.

reasons: rests on held decisions D-029 and D-060 (prior advance, trend template), kept out of the key

questions.q: Which trend does a VCP belong in?
questions.why: A Stage 2 uptrend. Minervini goes long a Stage 2 uptrend and never against the long-term trend.
questions.lesson_line: Long VCPs belong in uptrends. Check the trend before the box.

wrong.A Stage 4 downtrend: Minervini goes short a Stage 4 downtrend. A long VCP does not belong there.
wrong.A sideways drift under the 200-day: Below the 200-day we do not buy. The long needs a trend under it.

questions.q: The app's market filter reads Red, its most cautious color. A perfect VCP breaks out. You buy it at full size.
questions.why: False. Red means we're mostly in cash. The filter is a guide, not a lock. But in Red the market can't carry breakouts, and even perfect bases fail when buyers aren't around. Full size into that is how a clean chart turns into a loss. I'd let it go and keep the cash for a better market.
questions.lesson_line: Red is mostly cash. A great chart can't fix a market with no buyers.
questions.simple: False. Red means mostly cash, and even perfect bases fail when buyers aren't around.

deeper.counter: Red doesn't say the pattern is bad. It says the market can't carry it. ChartMill puts it bluntly: in a negative market, even perfect VCPs fail en masse.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (D46) and the card's market reading line

questions.q: You're checking a VCP before the buy. What's the lowest RS rating you'll take?
questions.why: 80 or more, and in one of the strongest groups. RS ranks a stock's strength against all other stocks. We want leaders because a breakout needs buyers to carry it, and leaders already have them. A 90 is great, but we don't need it. Check the RS rating in our app before every buy.
questions.lesson_line: We buy leaders. RS 80 or more, in a strong group.

wrong.70 or more: That's Minervini's floor. We hold a higher line, 80 or more.
wrong.90 or more: A 90 is great, but we don't need it. 80 or more in a strong group does it.
wrong.60 or more: Way too low for a leader. We want 80 or more, in a strong group.

questions.simple: 80 or more, in a strong group. Leaders already have the buyers a breakout needs.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C31), which beats Minervini's floor of 70

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: We take no longs below the ___-day simple moving average.
questions.why: 200. We take no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long. The card says the same: price above the 200-day SMA at the buy. A close under it ends the VCP idea before the buy.
questions.lesson_line: No longs under the 200-day. A VCP has to pass that first.
questions.simple: The 200-day average. We do not buy a long that sits below it.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)

questions.q: If the pullbacks in a base stop shrinking, it is not a VCP.
questions.why: True. A contraction as deep as, or deeper than, the one before ends the VCP idea. The contractions must shrink.
questions.lesson_line: No shrinking, no VCP. A wide and loose base waits.

questions.q: Which floor applies to a VCP we buy?
choices: $5 a share and $5 million a day
$10 a share and $20 million a day
No floor if the base is tight
$10 a share, with any dollar volume
questions.answer: $10 a share and $20 million a day
questions.why: $10 a share and $20 million a day. UCT trades only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. Both tests apply. The floor is the same for every setup, however tight the chart.
questions.lesson_line: Thin, cheap stocks are off the list however tight the chart.

wrong.No floor if the base is tight: A tight chart on a thin stock is still a pass.
wrong.$10 a share, with any dollar volume: Both tests apply. The stock must also trade at least $20 million a day.

questions.simple: Trade only stocks that cost at least $10 and trade at least $20 million a day. A tight chart changes nothing.

reasons: +3 one cited fact only (h09)
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B23)

questions.q: The first pullback is 24%. Each next one is half the last. How deep is the third?
questions.why: Halve the 24% once for the second pullback, then halve that result for the third, which gives 6%. Minervini likes each contraction to be about half of the one before, give or take. That is a rule of thumb, so real bases land near it, not exactly on it.
questions.lesson_line: About half each time. The swings shrink fast.
questions.simple: Halve the 24 percent once, then halve the result again. That leaves 6 percent for the third pullback.

deeper.example: Minervini's classic progression runs from a 25 percent correction to 10 percent to 5 percent. Those steps are not exact halves. His rule of thumb is about half, give or take. Use half as a guide, not a fixed ratio.

reasons: +2 a computed key
+2 sits beside the held decision D-059 on the contraction ratio
+1 fixed before

wrong.12%: That stops after one halving. It is the second pullback.
wrong.3%: That halves three times. The third pullback is two halvings in.
wrong.8%: That divides 24 by 3. Each pullback is half the last.

questions.q: The final contraction's high is 170.00 and its low is 164.05. How deep is it, in percent of the high?
questions.why: The depth is the high minus the low, divided by the high: (170.00 minus 164.05) divided by 170.00 is 3.5%. ChartMill wants the final contraction under 10%, and 3% to 6% is best. Our card says 10% or less.
questions.lesson_line: Depth is high minus low, divided by the high. The last swing should be the tightest.
questions.simple: Take the high minus the low, then divide by the high. For 170.00 and 164.05 that is 3.5 percent.

reasons: +2 a computed key

wrong.6.0%: That is the dollar amount read as a percent. Divide it first.
wrong.96.5%: That is the low as a share of the high, not the drop.

questions.q: How far is your stop from your fill, in percent?
questions.why: 2.7%. Take the fill minus the stop: 170.00 minus 165.39 is about 4.6 dollars. Divide that by the fill, 170.00, and you get 2.7%. Always divide by your fill, not the stop. That's right in the 1-3% range I like. Check this before you size, because the stop sets your share count.
questions.lesson_line: Know your stop in percent before you size. Under 3% is where I like it.
questions.simple: About 2.7 percent. That's a tight stop, and the stop is what sets your size.

reasons: +2 a computed key
+2 sits beside the held decision D-005 on stop width

wrong.4.6%: That's the dollar gap, about 4.6, read as a percent. Divide it by the fill first.
wrong.27.1%: A decimal slip. Recheck where the point goes.
wrong.97.3%: That's the stop as a share of the fill. You want the gap between them.

questions.story: You bought the breakout at 170.00. Your stop sits at 165.39, a few cents under the low of the day.

Somewhere between 2R and 5R, or at your first sell, the stop can come up to breakeven. Exactly when is a judgment call. From there the trade can't turn into a loser.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 2R before the open. Between 2R and 5R, breakeven comes into play.
questions.simple: Two R is two times your risk per share, added to the fill. Between 2R and 5R the stop can go to breakeven.

+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, the hard rule of a third at 3R)

wrong.$18.17: That counts two R up from the stop, not from your fill.
wrong.$18.96: That's the 2R mark: your fill plus two R.
wrong.$19.38: That adds 2 dollars. R is your risk per share, the fill minus the stop.
wrong.$19.75: That's 3R. Count two R, not three.

questions.story: You bought the breakout at 17.38. Your stop is 16.59, a few cents under the low of the day.

questions.q: We never pay more than 4% over the pivot. What's the most you'll pay, to the cent?
questions.why: $17.13. Take the pivot times 1.04: 16.47 times 1.04 is 17.13. Above that you're chasing. Your stop doesn't move up with you, so every cent past the pivot makes the stop wider and your share count smaller. Write 17.13 in your plan the night before. If it's already past that when you look, you don't buy it there.
questions.lesson_line: Write the chase limit down before the open. 4% over the pivot, no further.
questions.simple: 17.13. Past that you're chasing, and the stop stays put, so your shares shrink.

deeper.trap: Don't mix up two limits. The chase limit is 4% above the buy point. The stretch limit is separate: skip a long more than 10% above its 9 EMA. A buy has to pass both.

reasons: +2 a computed key
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C28)

wrong.$16.54: A decimal slip. That's only a few cents over the pivot.
wrong.$15.81: That's 4% under the pivot. The limit sits above it.

questions.story: The pivot on this base is 16.47. You plan to buy it tomorrow as it trades through.

questions.q: What's the play here?
choices: Pass, it's over 4% past the pivot
Buy it, the volume is strong
Buy half now, half on a dip
Buy it with a smaller size
questions.answer: Pass, it's over 4% past the pivot
questions.why: Pass. 26.10 is more than 4% over the 24.80 pivot, so you'd be chasing. Your stop stays under the buy point. The further you chase, the wider it gets and the fewer shares you can own. Heavy volume is nice, but it doesn't move the line. Let it go and wait for the next setup.
questions.lesson_line: Missed it by more than 4%, let it go. Another setup comes.

wrong.Buy it, the volume is strong: Volume raises the grade. It doesn't lift the 4% line.
wrong.Buy half now, half on a dip: We don't scale in. One full buy at one price, one stop.
wrong.Buy it with a smaller size: Smaller size keeps the dollar risk, but past 4% it's still a chase. The line is firm.

questions.simple: Pass. It's past 4 percent over the pivot, so you'd be chasing, and your shares shrink as the stop gets wider.

questions.q: Check the last swing on the right side of this base. It's the tightest one in the whole base.
questions.why: True. TRV pulled back 14.3%, then 6.4%, then just 3.4% right before the breakout. By the last swing the sellers are mostly gone, so price barely moves. That tight swing is what I want to see. It sets the pivot, and it keeps your stop close, so the risk is small. A loose last swing means a wide stop.
questions.lesson_line: The last swing is the tightest. That's where the pivot and the stop come from.
questions.simple: True. The last swing meets the fewest sellers, so it's the smallest, and it keeps your stop close.

reasons: final contraction at most 10% is a proposed card criterion

questions.q: What's the volume telling you?
questions.why: Sellers are drying up. Look how quiet the bars get as the swing tightens. The people who wanted out have mostly sold, so few shares change hands. With little supply left, it doesn't take much buying to push through the pivot. PHM did it the next day on 2.0x volume. I like seeing the dry-up because it raises the grade. It's not a must though.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet price, quiet volume. Volume dries up into the last swing.

wrong.Buyers are losing interest: Quiet on a pullback means sellers left, not buyers. Buyers show up at the pivot.
wrong.A breakdown is coming: A breakdown shows up as heavy selling. These bars are quiet.
wrong.Nothing, volume doesn't matter: It matters. It's not a must, but a dry-up raises the grade.

questions.simple: Sellers are drying up. Few shares trade because the people who wanted out are gone.

reasons: the specifics rest on one card line (c05)
volume_dry is a proposed criterion

questions.story: The day before the breakout. Check the volume bars under the last, tight swing.

questions.q: Is this base tightening the way a VCP should?
choices: No; the second swing barely shrank
Yes; the second swing is smaller
No; the first swing is too shallow
questions.answer: No; the second swing barely shrank
questions.why: No. Minervini likes each contraction to be about half the one before. Here 9.0% is most of 11.5%, so the sellers have not thinned out. ChartMill: what matters is that the pullbacks contract. This base stayed wide and loose.
questions.lesson_line: Swings that barely shrink make a loose base, not a VCP.

wrong.Yes; the second swing is smaller: It is smaller, but barely. A VCP needs each swing clearly smaller than the last.
wrong.Yes; two swings are enough: Two swings can make a VCP, but only when the second is clearly smaller.
wrong.No; the first swing is too shallow: 11.5% is a normal first swing. The trouble is that the second barely shrank.

questions.story: The day before it trades through its pivot. The base has two pullbacks, 11.5% then 9.0%.
questions.simple: No. The second swing is nearly as big as the first, so the sellers have not thinned out.

reasons: wide-and-loose invalidation is a proposed card criterion
the story uses equal swings against a ratio that is a held decision (D-059)

questions.q: Which setup is this?
questions.why: A flat base. One box where the swings stay the same size has no real volatility contraction. Minervini describes a flat base of four to seven weeks as a tight, narrow box. This one rests six weeks after a 40% run. A VCP's pullbacks shrink one after another, and this box has none that do.
questions.lesson_line: Same-size swings are a box. Shrinking swings are a VCP.

wrong.A VCP: A VCP needs successive pullbacks that shrink. These do not.
wrong.A high tight flag: A high tight flag follows a run of 90% or more in 8 weeks or less. This run was 40% over four months.
wrong.A cup with handle: A cup is one rounded decline and one handle at the rim. This is a flat box.

questions.story: After a 40% run over four months, a leader rests six weeks in a 10% range. The swings inside stay about the same size.
questions.simple: A flat base. The swings stay about the same size, so nothing is shrinking the way it does in a VCP.

deeper.counter: A tight box can still break out, and that does not turn it into a VCP. A flat base has no shrinking pullbacks and breaks out above the base high. A VCP is defined by the shrinking, not by the breakout.

reasons: +2 rests on the held decisions D-002, D-042 and D-043 (flat base against VCP, length and depth)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: By our rule, which base is the VCP?
choices: Base B; its pullbacks get smaller
Base A; one deep pullback is enough
Both; each pulls back and recovers
Neither; a VCP needs a cup shape first
questions.answer: Base B; its pullbacks get smaller
questions.why: Base B. A VCP strings pullbacks that shrink one after another, from greater volatility on the left to lesser on the right: 18%, 9%, 4%. Base A has one pullback, so nothing shrinks.
questions.lesson_line: A VCP is a string of shrinking pullbacks. One pullback is not a string.

wrong.Both; each pulls back and recovers: Every base pulls back. A VCP needs pullbacks that shrink one after another.
wrong.Base A; one deep pullback is enough: One pullback has nothing to shrink. A VCP needs a string of them.
wrong.Neither; a VCP needs a cup shape first: A cup is a different base: one rounded decline and one handle. A VCP is read by its shrinking pullbacks.

questions.story: Base A has one 15% pullback, then drifts up to the pivot. Base B has three pullbacks: 18%, 9% and 4%.
questions.simple: Base B is the VCP, because its three pullbacks keep shrinking, while Base A has only one pullback.

reasons: count questions sit near the held decision D-058 (contraction count), kept out of the key
key rests on one card line (c33) plus a general Minervini line

questions.q: Buy or pass?
choices: Wait a day and buy at the open
questions.why: Pass. The entry day's low is already under the final contraction's low, so the base has broken and there is no trade. ChartMill: if price drops below that low, the final contraction has failed to hold and the premise of the trade is gone. Clearing the pivot is not enough, and a wider stop does not fix a broken base.
questions.lesson_line: The structure comes first. If the day's low breaks the last swing's low, there is no trade.

wrong.Buy; it cleared the pivot: Clearing the pivot is only half the test. The final low must hold.
wrong.Buy with a wider stop: Widening the stop is a named mistake. The structure failed.
wrong.Wait a day and buy at the open: Waiting a day does not repair a broken base. By our rule there is no trade.

questions.story: Price trades through the pivot at 11:00. The day's low so far is already under the final contraction's low.
questions.simple: Pass. The day's low is under the last swing's low, so the base has broken and a wider stop will not fix it.

reasons: +2 keys a proposed card check (vcp.stop_structure_check) beside the held decision D-008

questions.q: What do you do with it?
choices: Hold, the stop is the exit
Move the stop down for room
Sell it all at the open
questions.answer: Hold, the stop is the exit
questions.why: Hold. A breakout day that closes back inside the base is a squat. Sellers shoved it back, and that's a real warning. But a warning isn't the exit. Your stop at 27.70 is. On ALGN the next day traded 27.64 and took it. A planned loss of about 3.3%, and you move on to the next one.
questions.lesson_line: A squat is a warning. The stop is the exit.

wrong.Add more, it's cheaper now: It's back under your buy, so that's adding to a loser. Never. One full buy, one stop.
wrong.Move the stop down for room: The stop only moves up, never lower.
wrong.Sell it all at the open: A squat is a warning, not an exit. The stop decides.

questions.story: You bought the breakout at 28.65, stop 27.70. By the close it's back at 28.14, inside the base, still above your stop.
questions.simple: Hold. A close back in the base is a warning, but the stop is what gets you out.

deeper.counter: A warning isn't a shrug. In our scan of past VCP buys, a squat reached 3R about half as often. A close above the pivot did twice as well. So the squat is real, but the stop still decides the exit.

questions.q: Do you buy it today?
choices: No, wait until after the report
questions.answer: No, wait until after the report
questions.why: No. We don't open new buys in the 3 days before a report, and this one reports tomorrow. Earnings can gap a stock right through your stop overnight, and a stop can't stop a gap. Half size still eats that gap. After the report, if it sets up again, you buy the new trigger. We only hold through a report when the trade's already up 5R.
questions.lesson_line: Check the report date before every buy. Inside 3 days, you wait.

wrong.Yes, the setup is perfect: A perfect chart doesn't stop an earnings gap. No new buys in the 3 days before.
wrong.Yes, but at half size: Half size still takes the gap. The rule is no new buy, not a smaller one.
wrong.No, drop it for good: It's a wait, not a ban. After the report it can set up again.

questions.story: The last swing is tight, volume dried up, and price trades through the pivot at 11 a.m. Earnings come out tomorrow morning.
questions.simple: No. A report can gap the stock right past your stop, so we don't open new buys right before one.

reasons: +3 one cited fact only (h08)
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)

questions.q: You bought a VCP breakout three days ago. It closes under the 20 EMA but stays above your stop. That's a warning, not a sell.
questions.why: True. Losing the 20 EMA right after a breakout says the move is stalling, so I watch it closer. But your stop is still the exit, and it already caps the loss. Sell on every wobble and you'll cut the winners that dip and recover. The 20 EMA matters more later, once you've sold some. Then a close under your trail sells what's left.
questions.lesson_line: Warnings tell you to watch closer. The stop tells you to get out.
questions.simple: True. It's a warning to watch, but your stop is the exit and it already caps the loss.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A4) and a proposed card warning

questions.q: What are the lows telling you?
choices: The base is about to break down
questions.why: Buyers are stepping in sooner. The last dip bottomed well above the base's lowest low. People who missed it the first time are willing to pay up now. That's demand showing itself before the breakout. GXO's swings went 22.3%, 9.3%, then 5.2%, and it cleared 54.13 the next day. Higher lows and a tighter range, that's what I want to see.
questions.lesson_line: Higher lows and a tighter range. That's demand showing up early.

wrong.Sellers are taking over: Sellers in charge push each low lower. These lows hold higher.
wrong.The base is about to break down: A breakdown starts with lower lows. This base is doing the opposite.
wrong.Nothing, only the highs matter: The lows matter as much. Higher lows show demand coming in early.

questions.simple: Buyers are stepping in sooner. The last dip stopped well above the base low, so demand is showing up early.

reasons: key rests on one card line (c04)
the second source describes a different setup
higher_lows is a proposed criterion

questions.story: The day before a breakout. Compare where each pullback in this base bottomed out.

questions.q: Which setup is this?
choices: A flat base after a rally
questions.why: A high tight flag. The stock doubled in 7 weeks, a very big run in a short time, then paused with no shrinking pullbacks. On our card, a high tight flag follows a run of 90% or more in 8 weeks or less, then pauses 5 to 30 sessions, at most 25% deep. A VCP needs pullbacks that shrink one after another.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the pole first. A near-double that pauses is a high tight flag.

wrong.A VCP in the making: A VCP shows pullbacks that shrink one after another. This is one quiet pause after a double.
wrong.A flat base after a rally: A run of 90% or more in 8 weeks or less, then a pause, is a high tight flag. It is not a flat base.
wrong.A cup with a handle: A cup is one rounded decline and one handle at the rim. This is a quick pause after a double.

questions.story: A stock doubles in 7 weeks, then pauses for 18 sessions, 8% deep, with no shrinking pullbacks.
questions.simple: A high tight flag. The stock doubled in 7 weeks and then paused, and a VCP would show shrinking pullbacks instead.

reasons: +3 one cited fact only (c34)
+2 rests on the held decisions D-048, D-049 and D-050
+1 fixed before

questions.q: By our rule, which test fails?
choices: The first pullback is too deep
The first pullback is too shallow
The last pullback is too wide
questions.answer: The last pullback is too wide
questions.why: The last pullback is too wide. Our rule allows at most 10% for the final contraction, and 11.5% is more. The 24% first pullback is inside the 10% to 40% range, so that test passes. Our BIIB read had a 24% first leg and an 11.5% final leg and was called a loose cup.
questions.lesson_line: The last swing has to be the tightest. 11.5% is still loose.

wrong.The first pullback is too deep: A 24% first leg is inside the 10% to 40% range. The last swing is the problem.
wrong.The first pullback is too shallow: 24% clears the 10% floor for a first pullback. The last swing is the problem.
wrong.Nothing; 11.5% is about half of 24%: Half is the rule of thumb for each step, but the final swing must also be at most 10%, and 11.5% is not.

questions.story: The day before a breakout. The base has two pullbacks: about 24%, then 11.5%.
questions.simple: The final contraction fails, because the rule allows at most 10% and the last pullback here is 11.5%.

deeper.counter: Halving is not enough on its own. Minervini likes each contraction to be about half of the one before, and 24% then 11.5% is about that. The base still fails, because the final contraction has its own ceiling of 10% or less.

reasons: final at most 10% is a proposed criterion
the BIIB example comes from our own scan, not reviewed by the owner

questions.q: What is missing?
choices: A dry-up in the last swing's volume
questions.answer: A dry-up in the last swing's volume
questions.why: A dry-up. The final leg traded above the 50-day average volume with no quiet day. The rule needs below 1x and a day at 0.5x or under.
questions.lesson_line: Shrinking swings are not enough. Volume has to dry up too.

wrong.The pullbacks are not shrinking: They shrink from 14% to 4%. That part passes.
wrong.The pivot is too high: The pivot is not the issue. The volume is.

questions.story: Two pullbacks shrink from 14% to 4%. But the final leg traded at 1.13x the 50-day average volume, with no quiet day.

questions.q: What is it really?
choices: A flat base, by Minervini's waiver
questions.answer: A flat base, by Minervini's waiver
questions.why: A flat base. A first contraction of 9.1% is too shallow to contract from. Minervini's waiver says a base under 10% deep needs no contraction.
questions.lesson_line: A base that shallow is already tight. Judge it by the flat base rules.

wrong.A textbook VCP: The first contraction is under the 10% line, so it is not a VCP.
wrong.A cup with handle: There is no rounded decline here. It is a shallow rest.

questions.story: A leader's first pullback is only 9.1% deep. The next one is smaller still, and the stock breaks out.

questions.q: Do you buy it?
choices: Buy it, and note the heavy day
Pass, that day kills the setup
Buy it with a wider stop
Wait for a whole new base
questions.answer: Buy it, and note the heavy day
questions.why: Buy it, and make a note. One heavy down day means a seller showed up. That's a distribution day, so I'm more mindful of it. It can lower the grade, and a lower grade can mean a smaller size. But it doesn't kill the setup. Most of the time one day like that doesn't matter. Several of them is different. Then big sellers are still around and I'd be a lot pickier.
questions.lesson_line: One heavy down day is a note on the chart, not a reason to pass.

wrong.Pass, that day kills the setup: One heavy day is a warning, not a veto. The setup is still valid.
wrong.Buy it with a wider stop: The stop never widens for a worry. It goes a few cents under the low of the day.
wrong.Wait for a whole new base: Nothing here has failed. Skipping a valid trigger over one day gives up the trade.

questions.story: A VCP trades through its pivot in regular hours. The swings shrank and the base is tight. Back in the right half, one down day came on heavy volume.
questions.simple: Buy it and note the heavy day. One day of selling is a warning and maybe a lower grade, not a pass.

reasons: the heavy-down-day rule is the owner's 2026-11-14 ruling VCP-HEAVY: a warning and a lower grade, never an invalidation
ChartMill's 'several days' is a caution, not a gate

questions.q: This VCP broke out today on light volume, 0.7x its average. You should sell it before the close.
questions.why: False. Light volume is a yellow flag and it lowers the grade. It's not an exit. The stop is. Volume often comes in a day or two later. NKE broke out on 0.7x and still got to 3R in 13 days. Sell every light breakout and you'll miss trades like that. Keep the stop under the low of the day and let it prove itself.
questions.lesson_line: Light volume lowers the grade. The stop is still the exit.
questions.simple: False. Light volume lowers the grade, but your stop decides when you sell, not the volume.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A4) and sits beside the held decision D-006 on breakout volume
+1 fixed before

questions.q: When do we look at pulling the stop up to breakeven?
questions.why: Between 2R and 5R, or at your first sell. Breakeven means this trade can't turn into a loser anymore. Do it too early, under 2R, and a normal pullback shakes you out of a good trade. Wait way past 5R and the stop under your entry gives back too much. At 3R you're in the window. Exactly where is a judgment call.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell. The stop only moves up.

wrong.Between 1R and 2R: Too early. Normal noise takes you out before the trade has room.
wrong.Between 5R and 8R: Too late. A stop still under the entry gives back way too much by then.
wrong.Between 8R and 10R: Way too late. Most of that open gain could go right back.

questions.story: You bought a VCP breakout. The stop is still a few cents under the entry day's low. It has run up 3R.
questions.simple: Between 2R and 5R, or at your first sell. Then a winner can't turn back into a loser.

reasons: rests on the rulebook (B19), whose wording is 'ideally' within a window
the old key said 'by default at the first trim', which no quoted line states

questions.q: Which one is the cleaner VCP?
questions.why: A, and it's not close. Each of A's swings is about half the one before: 24, 12, 6, 3. The sellers keep thinning out, and that 3% last swing gives you a tight stop. B's second swing is still 17%, most of the first. It's wide and loose, and a stop there sits a long way down. A cleaner base earns a higher grade and a bigger size. Grading is still my judgment, not a formula.
questions.lesson_line: The cleaner base keeps getting tighter. Tighter means a closer stop and a higher grade.

wrong.B, it has fewer swings: Fewer swings isn't cleaner. B's second swing is still most of its first.
wrong.They're about equally clean: A gets down to 3%. B only gets to 17%. That's a big difference.
wrong.Neither, both are too deep: A 24% first pullback is fine for a leader. What matters is that the last swing gets tight.

questions.story: Two bases. A pulls back 24%, then 12%, 6% and 3%. B pulls back 24%, then 17%. Our grade is how clean we judge a setup, and it sets the size.
questions.simple: A. Its swings keep halving down to 3 percent, while B's second swing is still 17 percent.

reasons: +2 rests on the held decisions D-058 (how many contractions) and D-059 (the ratio)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: Looking back, where should your stop have been?
choices: Raised the day after it broke
questions.why: Where it started, 505.97. The trade topped at 1.18R, short of 2R, so it never earned a breakeven stop. Pull it up early and normal noise shakes you out of trades that are still working. The 3.2% stop did its job and capped the loss right where the plan said. META hit it five sessions later, with a low of 494.23. Small loss, on to the next.
questions.lesson_line: 1.18R hasn't earned breakeven. Until it does, the first stop is the exit.

wrong.Up at breakeven, 522.89: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R, or at a first sell. This one topped at 1.18R with no sell.
wrong.Just under the 20 EMA: The 20 EMA is a trail for later, after a first sell. It's not your starting stop.
wrong.Raised the day after it broke: A breakout alone doesn't earn a higher stop. It has to work first.

questions.story: You bought the breakout at 522.89, stop 505.97. It got up to 1.18R, then faded for five sessions back toward your stop.

questions.q: What did you do wrong?

The stop was 4.6% under the buy, so the loss was small and planned. The winners pay for these. Take the loss and look for the next one.
questions.lesson_line: A clean setup can still lose. The stop is the cost of finding out.

wrong.Bought on light volume: 2.0x the average is heavy, not light.
wrong.Bought too shallow a base: Those swings are normal for a VCP. Nothing there was off.

questions.story: You bought at 27.60, stop 26.32. Two shrinking pullbacks, 14.2% then 4.6%, a breakout on 2.0x volume and a close above the pivot. It got to 0.87R, then fell to your stop.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, the stop is the exit)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: How many shares do you buy?
questions.why: 201 shares. Your risk is 0.5% of $100,000, which is $500. Your risk per share is 125.23 minus 122.75, about two and a half dollars. Divide $500 by that and round down, and you get 201. If it hits the stop you lose about $500, which is the plan. Tight stop or wide stop, the dollars at risk stay the same. Only the share count changes.
questions.lesson_line: Shares come from the stop. Dollars at risk divided by risk per share, rounded down.
questions.simple: 201. Take the dollars you're risking, divide by the risk per share, and round down.

reasons: +2 a computed key
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, shares rounded down then capped)

wrong.500 shares: That's your dollar risk, not shares. Divide it by the risk per share.
wrong.403 shares: That's double the 0.5% you planned to risk.
wrong.100 shares: That's half the risk you planned.

questions.story: You buy the breakout at 125.23 with your stop at 122.75. The account is $100,000 and you risk 0.5% on this one.

questions.q: Your VCP breaks out and works. You plan to add more shares on each new high. That's how we build the position.
questions.why: False. We make one full buy, at one price, with one stop. No pilot buys, and adding is never the plan. Adding to a working winner happens, but it's rare and a feel call. Every add comes in higher, so your average cost climbs and the cushion over your stop shrinks. Then a normal pullback can turn a winner into a loser. The size is set by the stop before you buy, so get it right then.
questions.lesson_line: One full buy, one stop. We don't build it in pieces.
questions.simple: False. We make one full buy with one stop, because adding higher raises your cost and shrinks your cushion.

reasons: rests on the rulebook (A5)

questions.q: Your VCP is a fast mover and you've sold part. Which line do you trail what's left with?
questions.why: The 9 EMA. A fast mover rides close to its 9 EMA, so a close under it tells you the run has changed. That's when you sell what's left. A steadier stock gets more room on the 20 EMA. The 50-day is too far back for a runner. You'd give up too much of the move.
questions.lesson_line: Fast mover, trail the 9 EMA. Steadier, trail the 20 EMA.

wrong.The 50-day: Too far back. A runner gives back a lot before it closes under the 50.
wrong.The 200-day: The 200-day is our trend line for new buys, not a trail.
wrong.The 20 EMA: That's for steadier movers. A fast one trails the 9 EMA.

questions.simple: The 9 EMA. A fast mover hugs it, so a close below it says the run has changed.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (E52)

questions.q: What's the play?
choices: Sell it, free up the money
questions.answer: Sell it, free up the money
questions.why: Sell it. Ten trading days and still under 1R means it isn't doing what a breakout should. That money could be in a fresh setup that's actually moving. A good-looking base doesn't change that. The time stop is there so dead money doesn't sit around in your account.
questions.lesson_line: Under 1R after 10 days, it's dead money. Sell it.

wrong.Hold, the base was perfect: The time stop doesn't care how the base looked.
wrong.Stop to breakeven and hold: Breakeven is for 2R to 5R. This is 0.5R after 10 days, so it goes.
wrong.Add while it's quiet: Adding to dead money just ties up more of it. This one goes.

questions.story: You bought a VCP breakout 10 trading days ago. It's gone sideways and sits up 0.5R.
questions.simple: Sell it. A trade doing nothing for 10 days ties up money a fresh setup could use.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C33)

questions.q: How do you handle the exit?
choices: Hold and wait for the gap to fill
Keep the old stop, wait it out
questions.why: Use the gap rule. A gap can jump right over your stop, and no order fixes that. So on a gap through the stop, the low of the first 30-minute bar becomes your new stop. If those first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, you're out. AXON traded 592.76, way through a stop 0.3% under the 694.02 buy. That's why a tiny stop never earns a huge position.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through your stop gets the 30-minute rule. Past 2R, you're out.

wrong.Hold and wait for the gap to fill: Hoping for a fill isn't a plan. The gap rule sets a new stop.
wrong.Keep the old stop, wait it out: It's already through the old stop. The gap rule takes over.
wrong.Buy more, it's on sale: Never add to a loser. You're managing the exit, not buying more.

questions.story: You bought at 694.02. The low of the day was 691.86, so your stop sat just 0.3% under. The next day it opens lower and falls hard, as low as 592.76.
questions.simple: Use the gap rule. The first 30-minute low is your new stop, and past 2R you get out.

reasons: rests on the rulebook gap rule (B20)
the AXON numbers come from our own scan

questions.q: Which breakout day reached 3R more often in our scan?
choices: A close back inside the base
The day on the most volume
questions.why: A close above the pivot. In our scan, a close above the pivot on the buy day reached 3R 36.9% of the time, against 18.9% for a close back inside the base. This is our own scan of daily bars, not a rule. A close back inside (the squat) is a warning, not an exit by itself.
questions.lesson_line: How the breakout day closes matters. Back inside the base is the worst sign.

wrong.A close back inside the base: Those reached 3R about half as often.
wrong.No difference between them: The scan showed a clear gap.
wrong.The day on the most volume: The scan compared where the day closed, not volume. ALGN broke through on 2.3x volume, closed back inside the base and was stopped a session later.

questions.simple: A close above the pivot did better, reaching 3R 36.9% of the time against 18.9% for a close back inside.

deeper.example: ALGN shows the squat. On 2007-10-17 it went through the 28.64 pivot on 2.3x volume, but the day closed at 28.14, back inside the base. It was stopped one session later, on 2007-10-18, with a low of 27.64.

questions.q: What does this tell you?
questions.why: A squat. The breakout cleared 28.64 on 2.3x volume but closed at 28.14, back inside the base. The stop took it the next day.
questions.lesson_line: A volume surge that closes inside the base is a squat. Keep the stop.

wrong.A strong breakout; volume confirms: Volume confirmed nothing; the close gave it all back.
wrong.An A+ entry: A close back inside the base is the warning with the worst numbers.

questions.q: Buy at the pivot?
choices: No; wait for the base high
No; the base is too short
Yes; the pivot is the final swing's high
questions.answer: Yes; the pivot is the final swing's high
questions.why: Yes. The pivot is the final contraction's high, and it may sit below the base's high. JOYY's pivot was 51.22 under a base high of 56.75.
questions.lesson_line: The final swing's high is the pivot, even under the base high.

wrong.No; wait for the base high: Waiting for 56.75 means chasing the move. The pivot is the final swing.
wrong.No; the base is too short: Length is not the problem here.

questions.story: JOYY's base high is 56.75. Its final contraction tops out at 51.22, and the stock trades through 51.22 on heavy volume.

questions.q: What does it do to the grade?
choices: It raises it; a grade cue
questions.answer: It raises it; a grade cue
questions.why: It raises the grade. The dip under the low shakes out weak holders, and the same-day recovery shows buyers took the supply, so fewer sellers are left for the breakout. A recovered undercut and then a higher low is a plus in our judgment. A lower low, or no shakeout, is a weaker look.
questions.lesson_line: A shakeout that recovers, then a higher low, is a good sign.

wrong.It voids the setup: An undercut that recovers is a cue, not a failure.
wrong.It lowers it; low broke: A lower low would weaken the look. This one recovered, then made a higher low.
wrong.No change; it is noise: Our rule treats an undercut that recovers, then a higher low, as a grade cue. It is not noise.

questions.story: A grade is our judgment of how clean a setup is, and the grade sets the size. The last contraction dips under an earlier swing's low, closes back above it the same day, then forms a higher low.
questions.simple: It raises the grade. A dip that recovers shakes out weak holders, and the higher low after it shows buyers are in.

deeper.trap: Do not read every undercut as a good sign. The plus is an undercut that recovers and then makes a higher low. If the next low is lower, or there is no shakeout, the look is weaker.

reasons: rests on one card line (c09)
shakeout is a proposed criterion

questions.q: A breakout on light volume. What now?
choices: Add; the quiet is a bargain
Keep the stop and watch for volume
questions.answer: Keep the stop and watch for volume
questions.why: Keep the stop and watch for volume. Minervini: lack of volume raises a red flag, volume would need to come in soon after, and you maintain your stop regardless.
questions.lesson_line: Light volume is a red flag, not an exit. The stop is the exit.

wrong.Sell at once; no volume: The stop is the exit. Volume is a grade cue.

questions.story: A clean VCP breaks out on 0.7x average volume. It closes above the pivot.

questions.q: How does the base count change your read?
choices: Worse odds than an early base
Better odds, the trend is proven
questions.answer: Worse odds than an early base
questions.why: Worse odds. By the fourth base everyone has seen this stock run. The easy money's been made, and the base is obvious to the whole market. A first or second base after a new uptrend starts has better odds. I'd still look at it, but I'm a lot pickier on a late base and the grade comes down.
questions.lesson_line: First and second bases are the money bases. Late bases fail more.

wrong.Better odds, the trend is proven: A long run makes the base obvious to everyone. That's the risk.
wrong.Only matters on light volume: The base count is its own check, whatever the volume.
wrong.It doesn't, clean is clean: A clean shape doesn't fix a late stage. Late bases fail more often.

questions.story: A leader has run for two years. Now it's building its fourth base, and the pattern looks clean.
questions.simple: Worse odds. A late base is obvious to everyone, so it fails more often than a first or second.

deeper.trap: A clean shape on a late base is the lure. Minervini warns that a late-stage base is obvious to everyone and prone to failure. ChartMill gives a third or fourth base worse odds than a first or second.

The close back under the pivot

Buy, the 10% line is for chases
Pass, the base is too loose

deeper.trap: The trap is the clean breakout. The pivot, the volume and the base can all pass. The trade is still a skip, because the stretch is measured from the 9 EMA, not the pivot.
