questions.q: Do you take it?
choices: Pass, too cheap and too thin
questions.answer: Pass, too cheap and too thin
questions.why: Pass. We only trade stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. This one fails both. In a thin name you can't get out at your stop without moving the price yourself. The loss you planned isn't the loss you get. Illiquid stocks aren't even on our watchlist. Check price and dollar volume before you look at the pattern.
questions.lesson_line: Price and liquidity come first. Then the chart.

wrong.Take it, the pattern's clean: The pattern doesn't matter if you can't get out. Thin names aren't even watched.
wrong.Pass, price must be over $20: Right call, wrong number. It's $10 for price and $20 million a day for trading.
wrong.Take it at half size: Smaller size doesn't fix a thin stock. It fails both tests.

questions.story: A tight VCP breaks out in an $8 stock that trades about $5 million a day.
questions.simple: Pass. It's under $10 and trades well under $20 million a day, so you can't trust your exit.

deeper.trap: The two numbers are separate tests. A stock can clear $10 and still fail the $20 million a day test, or the other way round. A clean pattern is the lure, and the floor comes first.

reasons: rests on the rulebook (B23, D42)

questions.q: Which ones do you buy?
choices: The A+ and the best B
questions.why: Only the A+. In Orange the market's under pressure and breakouts fail more often, because buyers aren't there to back them. So I only want my very best idea, the cleanest base with the tightest risk. The two B's can wait for a better market. Yellow is smaller and fewer. Green is when we press. Red is mostly cash.
questions.lesson_line: Orange, just the A+. Green, we press. Red, mostly cash.

wrong.All three, smaller size: Smaller and fewer is Yellow. Orange is the A+ only.
wrong.The A+ and the best B: In Orange even a good B waits.
wrong.None, wait for Green: Orange still allows the A+. Red is when we're mostly cash.

questions.story: The app's market filter (Green, Yellow, Orange, Red) turns Orange, one step from Red. Three VCPs trigger: one A+, our cleanest kind, and two B's.
questions.simple: Only the A+. In Orange fewer buyers are around, so only the cleanest setup gets your money.

deeper.trap: Yellow and Orange are different cuts. Yellow means smaller and fewer. Orange means A+ only, so both B grades wait. Red means mostly cash.

reasons: rests on the rulebook market reading (A10, F65)

questions.q: Do you buy it?
choices: Buy it, the chart is clean
questions.why: Pass. We want an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups. At 72 in a weak group, it misses on both. A breakout needs buyers to carry it, and leaders already have them. A laggard with a nice chart is still a laggard. I'd rather put the money in the strongest names.
questions.lesson_line: Buy leaders. A tight chart on a laggard can wait.

wrong.Buy it at half size: Half size doesn't make it a leader.
wrong.Buy it, the chart is clean: A clean chart on a laggard is still a laggard.
wrong.Buy, it clears Minervini's 70: His floor is 70. Ours is 80, in a strong group.

questions.story: A clean VCP sets up, but the stock sits in a weak group. Its RS rating, its strength rank against all other stocks, is 72.
questions.simple: Pass. It's 72 in a weak group, and we want 80 or more in a strong one.

deeper.counter: Minervini's floor is 70, preferably in the 90s. Ours is 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups. A stock can clear his floor and still miss ours.

reasons: rests on the rulebook leader rule (C31)

questions.q: Is the setup still on?
choices: Yes, the base is still tight
Yes, one close is just noise
Only off if volume was heavy
questions.why: No, it's off. Below the 200-day we don't buy stocks. That's a hard line. A close under it says the uptrend you were counting on isn't there right now. The base can look perfect and it doesn't matter. If it gets back over the 200-day and builds a new tight swing, you look again.
questions.lesson_line: Lose the 200-day and the setup's off, however good the base looks.

wrong.Yes, the base is still tight: Tight doesn't beat the trend. Under the 200-day it's off.
wrong.Yes, one close is just noise: We don't buy stocks under the 200-day, one close or ten.
wrong.Only off if volume was heavy: Volume has nothing to do with it. The close under the 200-day ends it.

questions.story: A base is coming together nicely. Then the stock closes below its 200-day.
questions.simple: No. Under the 200-day there's no uptrend, and we don't buy stocks there.

deeper.trap: A tight base isn't a trend. The base can look perfect while the trend fails. For a stock there's no way around the 200-day. Only indexes and levered ETFs may be bought under it, on a reversal extension or a parabolic long.

reasons: trend-template lines are a held decision (D-060), kept out of the key except the settled 200-day line

questions.q: What happens to the old pivot?
choices: It's void, wait for a new one
questions.answer: It's void, wait for a new one
questions.why: It's void. The last tight swing was supposed to be where the sellers ran out. A close under its low says they didn't. So the old pivot doesn't mean much anymore, and the count starts over. If it builds a new tight swing, that swing's high is your new pivot. The stock isn't dead, it just isn't ready.
questions.lesson_line: Close under the last swing's low and the count starts over.

wrong.It stands, buy through it: The structure broke. That pivot is gone.
wrong.The pivot moves down too: You wait for a new tight swing. You don't drag the old line down.
wrong.The stock's done for good: It can set up again. A new tight swing makes a new pivot.

questions.story: Before it ever triggers, the stock closes below the low of its last tight swing.
questions.simple: It's void. A close under the last swing's low means sellers aren't done, so wait for a new tight swing.

deeper.trap: The trap is waiting for the old pivot to come back into play. After a close under the last low, it doesn't matter. Watch for a new tight swing and use its high as the new pivot.

reasons: +2 rests on a proposed card line (c13) and the owner's rulebook (A4 stop only moves up)

questions.q: A stock down 70% from its high can still form a good VCP base.
questions.why: False. A VCP is a pause inside a prior uptrend, not a repair job. A stock down 70% has been in a downtrend, not resting, and we buy leaders. Minervini calls a VCP a pause within the context of a prior uptrend.
questions.lesson_line: A stock that has fallen far is damaged, not resting. A VCP is a pause in an uptrend.
questions.simple: False. A VCP is a pause in an uptrend, and a stock that has fallen that far is damaged, not resting.

deeper.trap: The trap is a cheap-looking chart. A big fall can leave a tight-looking base, but the stock is no longer a leader pausing. The trend check and the leader rule usually catch it too.

reasons: first-contraction limits are proposed card criteria

questions.q: How big is the position?
questions.why: 40% of the account. 1% risk on a 2% stop works out to 50% of the account. The cap is 40%, so 40% it is. You take the smaller of the two, every time. The reason is gaps. A tight stop looks safe, but a gap can jump right over it. Then the 1% you planned turns into a lot more. The cap keeps one bad gap from doing real damage.
questions.lesson_line: A tight stop can ask for a huge size. The 40% cap says no.

wrong.50% of the account: That's the risk math before the cap. You take the smaller number.
wrong.2% of the account: 2% is how far away the stop is, not the size.
wrong.1% of the account: 1% is what you risk, not the size.

questions.story: Account $100,000. You risk 1% with a stop 2% under your entry. The math says a position of 50% of the account. Our cap is 40%.
questions.simple: 40 percent. You take the smaller of the risk math and the cap, because a gap can jump a tight stop.

deeper.example: The cap, not the risk rule, sets the size here. A 1% risk on a 2% stop asks for 50% of the account, and the cap trims it to 40%. Check the volume cap too: the position is also at most 1% of average daily volume.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the rulebook sizing and cap (A5, A7), the 40% cap quoted only through the card line (c22)

questions.q: The day before the breakout. How would you describe this base?
choices: One deep drop and a short handle
questions.why: Shrinking swings, and volume dries up. RNG pulled back 16.6%, then 11.0%, then just 3.5%. On that last swing the volume fell to 0.46x the average. That's the picture you want: the sellers are gone. It broke out the next day on 2.4x volume. Count the swings first, then check the volume under the last one.
questions.lesson_line: Count the swings, then check the volume under the last one.

wrong.One deep drop and a short handle: That's a cup with a handle. This base has three pullbacks.
wrong.Equal swings, steady volume: The swings shrink. The last one is a fraction of the first.
wrong.Widening swings, rising volume: The opposite. The last swing is the smallest and the quietest.

questions.simple: Shrinking swings and volume that dries up. The pullbacks fall from 16.6 to 3.5 percent as sellers run out.

deeper.example: On the buy day the pivot was 169.99 and the stop 165.39, 2.7% under it. In our scan the trade reached 3R in 5 days.

reasons: the example comes from our own scan, not reviewed by the owner
the ratio of swings sits near the held decision D-059
the bars were not checked by the writer

questions.q: The pullbacks shrink, 14% then 4%, but volume on the last leg stays above average. What's that telling you?
choices: The base is done, buy it
questions.why: Sellers may still be around. The price looks tight, but the volume says otherwise. In a real dry-up the last leg goes quiet. AMZN's last leg ran 1.13x its 50-day average, and its quietest day was still 0.81x. Somebody was selling into it. Volume raises the grade, it doesn't make the call. So I'd still look at it, but it's a lower grade and I'd be pickier on the entry.
questions.lesson_line: Tight price isn't enough. I want the volume to dry up too.

wrong.The 4% leg is too deep: 4% is tight. The problem is the volume, not the price.
wrong.Volume doesn't matter here: It matters. A dry-up raises the grade, and this one never dried up.
wrong.The base is done, buy it: Busy volume on the last leg isn't a finished base. It's a lower grade.

questions.simple: Sellers may still be around. Tight price with busy volume is half the picture, so the grade comes down.

deeper.trap: Shrinking price alone is the trap. Swings of 14% then 4% look textbook. But Minervini ties the shrinking to a drop in volume at points, and this last leg shows none.

reasons: the example comes from our own scan, not reviewed by the owner
the dry-up specifics rest on one card line (c05)
the bars were not checked by the writer

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Check it, build your own plan
Copy the entry, stop and size
Buy half, set a stop later
Wait for a second video to agree
questions.answer: Check it, build your own plan
questions.why: Check it, then build your own plan. The video doesn't know your account or your risk. Their size came from their stop and their account, not yours. So you mark your own pivot and put your own stop under the low of the day. Then you size it from your own risk. Write it down before the open, and put the stop in with the broker.
questions.lesson_line: Someone else's alert isn't a plan. Your entry, your stop, your size.

wrong.Wait for a second video to agree: Two videos are still someone else's plan.
wrong.Copy the entry, stop and size: That's their plan, sized for their account. It's never yours.
wrong.Buy half, set a stop later: The stop comes first, and we make one full buy.

questions.story: A video shows a VCP breakout with an entry, a stop and a size. The chart looks great.
questions.simple: Build your own entry, stop and size. The video doesn't know your account.

deeper.trap: A great chart in someone else's post is the pull. Copying their numbers feels safe, but it's their plan, not yours. And every position needs a real stop order with the broker.

reasons: rests on the rulebook (F66, D39)

questions.q: What is your call?
choices: Buy it; the stock is a leader
Pass; Red means no VCP buys
questions.answer: Pass; Red means no VCP buys
questions.why: Pass. Red means no VCP buys. Even perfect VCPs fail en masse when buyers are missing.
questions.lesson_line: A great setup in a Red market waits. Cash is a position.

wrong.Buy a starter: A starter in a Red market is still a long.
wrong.Buy it; the stock is a leader: Leadership does not cancel a Red market.

questions.story: A textbook VCP is one tick from its pivot. The market reading is Red.

questions.q: Which base is cleaner?
choices: Base A: selling shakes out weak hands
Base B: a quiet right side
questions.answer: Base B: a quiet right side
questions.why: Base B. If price and volume do not quiet down on the right side, supply is still coming. A heavy down day in the right half ends the setup.
questions.lesson_line: A quiet right side is the clean one.

wrong.Base A: selling shakes out weak hands: Heavy selling on the right side is distribution.
wrong.Neither; volume does not matter: The right-side test is a gate.

questions.story: Two bases have the same three shrinking swings. In Base A one right-half down day came on heavy volume. Base B's right half is quiet.

questions.q: What does B have to deal with that A doesn't?
choices: Sellers waiting at the old high
A wider stop on the buy day
questions.answer: Sellers waiting at the old high
questions.why: Sellers at the old high. People who bought up there and sat through the drop may sell to get out even. A stock at a new high has nobody above it like that. So B has supply to chew through, and it can stall into that old high. It's not a ban though. JOYY's pivot at 51.22 sat under its 56.75 high, and it reached 3R in 1 day. Location matters. Weigh it in the grade.
questions.lesson_line: A pivot at new highs has clear air above it. A lower pivot has sellers to get through.

wrong.A wider stop on the buy day: The stop goes under the low of the day wherever the pivot is.
wrong.A tighter chase limit: The chase limit is 4% for every VCP.
wrong.Nothing, only the shape counts: Location matters big time. Sellers at the old high can cap the move.

questions.story: Two VCPs, same shape. A's pivot sits at an all-time high. B's pivot sits well below its old high on the left.
questions.simple: Sellers at the old high. Holders up there may sell into the rally, while a stock at a new high has none.

deeper.counter: Overhead supply is a risk to weigh, not a ban. JOYY is the proof: its pivot sat under the old high, as Minervini allows, and it still ran.

reasons: key rests on one card line (c08)
pivot_location is a proposed criterion
our own examples contradict the cue: the ten winners had pivots under the base high

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Wait; one full buy at the trigger
Buy all now at a tight stop
questions.answer: Wait; one full buy at the trigger
questions.why: Wait for the trigger. The plan is one full buy at one price with one stop, no pilot buys. Buying early in the base is a named mistake.
questions.lesson_line: No pilot buys. We buy the trigger, not the dream.

wrong.Buy half now: A pilot buy is not allowed.
wrong.Buy all now at a tight stop: Buying before the pivot breaks is a named mistake.

questions.story: A VCP is two days from its pivot. A friend says to buy half now and the other half at the breakout.

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Keep the stop, size to it
Widen it to give it room
Pull it in so the size fits
questions.answer: Keep the stop, size to it
questions.why: Keep the stop and size to it. The stop goes where the chart says you're wrong, and the size comes from that. Never the other way around. A wider stop doesn't make you safer. Keep the same shares and you just lose more when it's wrong. Pull it in to fit more shares and normal noise shakes you out. If the honest stop won't fit your risk at all, skip the trade.
questions.lesson_line: The stop doesn't bend to the size. The size bends to the stop.

wrong.Widen it to give it room: Giving it room is how a 1R loss turns into a 3R loss.
wrong.Pull it in so the size fits: That's backwards. The size bends to the stop, not the stop to the size.
wrong.Use a mental stop instead: A stop in your head sells nothing. Put a real order in with the broker.

questions.story: Your honest stop, a few cents under the low of the day, gives you a smaller position than you'd like. A friend says just use a wider stop.
questions.simple: Keep the stop where the chart puts it and buy fewer shares, or skip the trade if it won't fit.

deeper.trap: The trap is bending the stop to suit the size. Shares are the dollars at risk divided by the distance to the stop, so a wide stop just means fewer shares. Once you're in, the stop only moves up.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, A4, A5)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: A VCP is breaking out and the company's sales and earnings are growing fast. You still judge the chart first.
questions.why: True. We like growing sales and earnings. Growth is why big buyers might want the stock. The chart shows whether they're actually buying it right now. Great numbers on a broken chart is still a broken chart. So the base, the trend and the trigger come first, and growth is a plus on top.
questions.lesson_line: Earnings are a plus. The chart comes first.
questions.simple: True. Growth is a plus, but the chart shows what buyers are doing right now.

reasons: +3 one cited fact only (h40)
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (D40)

questions.q: What does our rule say about the buy?
choices: The earnings come first; buy it
Both count the same; buy half size
Buy bigger; growth is the edge
questions.why: Pass. We prefer growing sales and earnings, but the chart comes first. This base is wide and loose, and its pullbacks are not shrinking, so it is not a VCP. A contraction as deep as the one before ends the VCP idea. Size comes from the stop, not from growth.
questions.lesson_line: Strong earnings do not fix a loose chart. The chart comes first.

wrong.The earnings come first; buy it: Earnings are a preference. They do not replace the chart rules.
wrong.Both count the same; buy half size: The chart comes first, so they do not count the same. A base that is not contracting is not a VCP.
wrong.Buy bigger; growth is the edge: Size comes from the stop, not from growth. This base is not contracting, so it is not a VCP.

questions.story: A company posts fast sales and earnings growth. Its base is wide and loose, and the pullbacks are not shrinking.
questions.simple: Pass. Growing sales and earnings are a plus, but the chart comes first, and this base is not contracting.

deeper.trap: The trap is a great story on a loose chart. Growth is a preference. A base whose pullbacks are not shrinking fails the VCP test no matter how strong the earnings are.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (D40)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: A down day in the base's second half trades 3.3 million shares. The 50-day average is 2.2 million. How many times the average?
questions.why: Divide the day's volume by the average: 3.3 million divided by 2.2 million is 1.5. That meets our line for a heavy-volume down day, 1.5 times the 50-day average or more. On the right side of a base it is a day to note and a reason to grade the setup lower. It does not end the setup. Find it by comparing that day's volume bar with the 50-day average line on the chart.
questions.lesson_line: A right-side down day at 1.5 times the average or more is a heavy day to note, not a veto.
questions.simple: The volume is 1.5 times the 50-day average. That is a heavy day to note, not a reason to pass.

reasons: a computed key
the 1.5 line is the card's measure; the owner's VCP-HEAVY ruling (2026-11-14) makes a heavy day a warning, never a gate

wrong.0.5x: That is only the extra over the average, not the multiple.
wrong.1.1x: That is the gap in millions, not a multiple of the average.
wrong.0.7x: That flips the division. Put the day's volume on top.

questions.q: By our rule, one heavy-volume down day in the right half of a VCP voids the setup.
questions.why: False. A heavy-volume down day is a day the stock falls on 1.5 times its 50-day average volume or more. In the right half of the base it is a day to note, but it does not end the setup. Most of the time it does not matter. Treat it as a distribution day, meaning sellers were active. Be more mindful of it and grade the setup lower. Several such days together are a bigger warning.
questions.lesson_line: A heavy down day on the right side is a warning, not a veto.
questions.simple: False. A heavy down day on the right side is a warning to note, but it does not end the setup.

reasons: the heavy-down-day rule is the owner's 2026-11-14 ruling VCP-HEAVY: a warning, no gate
overlaps q72, which computes the same 1.5 line

questions.q: By our card's grade cues, which base rates higher?
choices: Base A; its closes stay tight
Base B; its closes show action
Base B; it shakes out weak hands
questions.answer: Base A; its closes stay tight
questions.why: Base A. Our card lists tight closes, with little change from one day to the next and from one week to the next in the final contraction, as a grade cue. Both bases have the same 5% depth and quiet volume, so the closes decide. Grading stays a judgment call.
questions.lesson_line: In the final contraction, tight closes day to day and week to week grade higher.

wrong.Base B; its closes show action: Loose closes rate lower. The cue is little change from one day to the next.
wrong.Neither; equal depth, equal grade: Both are 5% deep, but our card also looks at tight closes.
wrong.Base B; it shakes out weak hands: A shakeout is a different cue: an undercut that recovers. Jumpy closes are not that.

questions.story: Two bases end in a 5% final contraction on quiet volume. In base A the closes sit within a few cents day to day. In base B they jump around inside the range.
questions.simple: Base A grades higher because tight closes, with little change from day to day, are a grade cue in the final contraction.

reasons: rests on one card line (c07)
tight closes is a proposed grade cue

questions.q: Tight closes in the final contraction are a grade cue for a VCP, not a gate.
questions.why: True. The card lists tight closes as a grade cue. That means little change from one day to the next and from one week to the next in the final contraction. Tight closes help the grade and loose closes lower it. They do not pass or fail the setup by themselves.
questions.lesson_line: Tight closes make a final contraction grade higher.
questions.simple: True. Tight closes help the grade, but they do not pass or fail the setup by themselves.

reasons: +2 rests on a proposed card cue not yet ruled on by the owner

questions.q: What did the plan miss?
choices: A real stop order with the broker
A wider stop for the shakeout
A phone alert at the stop
questions.answer: A real stop order with the broker
questions.why: A real stop order with the broker. Writing the stop down is a plan, but only an order actually sells. Your stop was 16.59, and the stock went to 16.20 while you weren't looking. Nothing was there to get you out. Put the stop in the moment you're filled. From there it only ever moves up.
questions.lesson_line: A stop in your notes isn't a stop. Put the order in with the broker.

wrong.A wider stop for the shakeout: A wider stop isn't the fix. No order existed at all.
wrong.A phone alert at the stop: An alert tells you. It doesn't sell anything.
wrong.Buying it over two days: We make one full buy. The missing piece was the order.

questions.story: You buy a VCP breakout at 17.38 and write your stop, 16.59, in your notebook. At 11 a.m. it trades 16.20 while you're in a meeting.
questions.simple: A real stop order with the broker. A stop in your notes sells nothing when you're away.

deeper.trap: The trap is that the plan was written down. A written stop is a plan, and only an order is an exit.

reasons: rests on the rulebook (D41, A4)

questions.q: A price alert on your phone can stand in for a stop order with the broker.
questions.why: False. Our rule is a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head. An alert only tells you the price. It sells nothing if you look away.
questions.lesson_line: The stop is an order, not a habit of watching.
questions.simple: False. We keep a real stop order with the broker, because an alert only tells you the price and sells nothing.

reasons: +3 one cited fact only (h41)
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (D41)

questions.q: You bought 900 shares. You sold 300 on the first sell and 300 on a later sell. How many are left to trail?
questions.why: 900 minus 300 minus 300 leaves 300. Both sales are counted on the full 900, not on what is left. Those 300 shares that are left are trailed. When to sell each part is a judgment, but the arithmetic is fixed.
questions.lesson_line: Count each sale on the full position. Trail what is left.
questions.simple: Two sales of 300 from 900 shares leave 300. Those shares that are left go on the trail.

reasons: +2 a computed key
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (E51, marked adjustable)
+1 fixed before

wrong.100 shares: That is a third of the 300 left, not the shares left.
wrong.200 shares: That is a third of what was left after one sale.
wrong.150 shares: That divides 900 by six. The question gives two sales of 300.

questions.q: How many shares do you sell now, and what happens to the rest?
choices: Sell the 800 left to lock in
questions.why: Sell 400 more. The same number as the first sale is 400, so 400 go and 400 are left. What is left trails the 9 EMA for fast movers or the 20 EMA for steadier ones. We sell on a close below it. Selling at about 5 to 10R is often best, but when to sell is a judgment.
questions.lesson_line: Count each sale on the full position. What is left rides the trail.

wrong.Sell the 800 left to lock in: You chose to sell the same number as before, which is 400. Selling all 800 is more than that.
wrong.Sell 600 more; run the rest: The same number as before is 400, not 600.
wrong.Sell nothing; trail all 800: You chose to sell 400 now. Only the 400 that are left ride the trail.

questions.story: You bought 1,200 shares and sold 400 earlier, with the stop at breakeven. Price now touches 5R. You decide to sell the same number of shares again.
questions.simple: Sell 400 shares, the same as before, and trail the 400 that are left until they close below the trail.

deeper.trap: The trap is treating the sale as the finish line. Selling 400 leaves 400, and they stay on until a close below the trail average.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (E51, E52)

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Selling part on a gap over a trim level is a ___, never a rule.
questions.why: Judgment. A gap over a trim level is not an automatic sell. Selling part at the open is one choice you may make, never a rule.
questions.lesson_line: A gap over a trim level is your call, never a rule.
questions.simple: Judgment. Selling part on a gap is your call, never a rule.

reasons: +3 one cited fact only (h42)
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (F63)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: What does the plan say at the open?
choices: It's your call, sell part or hold
Wait for a dip back to 21.40
You must sell part at the open
questions.answer: It's your call, sell part or hold
questions.why: It's your call. A gap over your level isn't an automatic sell. Selling part at 22.10 banks more than the 21.40 you planned for. Holding lets a strong move keep running. Both are fine. I make that call on the day, from how strong the move looks and how much I still hold. It's judgment, not a rule.
questions.lesson_line: A gap over your sell level is a choice, not an order.

wrong.Wait for a dip back to 21.40: Waiting for a dip is a bet that it comes. No rule asks for it.
wrong.You must sell part at the open: Selling part into a gap is an option. It's never a rule.
wrong.Sell everything at the open: The plan sells part and trails the rest. Not everything.

questions.story: Your VCP is past day 3 and you've already sold part. Your next sell level is 5R, at 21.40. Today it gaps up and opens at 22.10.
questions.simple: Your call. Selling part banks a gain, and holding lets a strong move run.

deeper.trap: The trap is treating the gap as an order. The level is behind you, and selling part is one choice you can make.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (F63, E51)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: What do you do with the position?
choices: Sell a big part into it
Hold it all for the trail
questions.answer: Sell a big part into it
questions.why: Sell a big part into it. A climax run packs a lot of gain into a few days. That's when the position is worth the most, and when it can turn the fastest. I'd rather sell into that strength than give it back on the way down. How much is a judgment call. Trail what's left on the 9 EMA.
questions.lesson_line: Into a climax run, sell a big part. How much is your call.

wrong.Add, the move is strong: A climax is where we sell, not where we buy. Never add into a stretched run like this.
wrong.Sell a small piece, hold: A token trim leaves most of it exposed. A climax calls for a big part.
wrong.Hold it all for the trail: The trail is for what's left. Into a climax, sell a big part first.

questions.story: Your VCP winner goes into a climax run: three gaps up in five days, rising volume, and a huge range today.
questions.simple: Sell a big part. A climax packs a lot of gain into a few days, and it can turn fast.

deeper.trap: A strong leg feels like proof, so the pull is to add or sit tight. Into a climax run on your own long, sell a big part. How much is your call.

questions.q: What's your move?
questions.story: A leader with RS 90 in a strong group, above its 200-day. The market filter reads Green. The last swing is 4% deep. At 10:30 it trades through the 31.20 pivot to 31.45, with a stop 2% under. It's 3% over its 9 EMA. Earnings are 12 days out.
choices: Buy at market, stop under the low
Rest a limit at the pivot
Buy half now, half on a dip
questions.answer: Buy at market, stop under the low
questions.simple: Buy it at market. Everything checks out, and the stop goes a few cents under the low of the day.
questions.why: Buy it at market. Go through it and nothing breaks a rule. RS 90 clears our 80 line. It's over the 200-day. The stop's 2%, right in the 1-3% I like. Earnings are 12 days out, well past the 3-day window. It's 3% over the 9 EMA, nowhere near 10%. So you hit it at market and put the stop a few cents under the low of the day. One full buy.
questions.lesson_line: When it all checks out, don't overthink it. Market order, stop under the low.

wrong.Pass, earnings are too close: We only stand aside in the 3 days before a report. This one's 12 days away.
wrong.Rest a limit at the pivot: We market order our entries. A resting limit can miss the move.
wrong.Buy half now, half on a dip: We don't scale in. One full buy, one stop.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (E57 market orders, A3 stop, B22 earnings window)

questions.q: Do you buy the breakout?
questions.story: A textbook VCP: shrinking swings, a 5% last swing, volume dried up. It trades through the 42.00 pivot at 42.15. The 200-day sits overhead at 43.00.
choices: Buy, it's only a hair under
Pass, the last swing is too wide
questions.why: Pass. Below the 200-day we don't buy stocks, and 42.15 is under 43.00. That's a hard line. Under its 200-day a stock isn't in an uptrend, however clean the pattern looks. Put an alert at 43.00. If it gets back over the 200-day and sets up again, you can look at it then.
questions.lesson_line: A clean pattern under the 200-day is still a pass.
questions.simple: Pass. It's under the 200-day, so it's not in an uptrend, however clean the base looks.

wrong.Buy, it's only a hair under: There's no close enough. Under the 200-day is a no.
wrong.Buy half until it clears 43: The 200-day isn't a size cue. Under it, we don't buy the stock at all.
wrong.Pass, the last swing is too wide: 5% is a tight last swing. The 200-day is the problem.

questions.q: Do you take your first sell here?
questions.story: You bought a VCP breakout, stop under the low of the day. By day 2 it's already up 3R.
choices: Not yet, wait for day 3 or later
Yes, sell a third, 3R is the rule
Yes, sell it all and bank it
Sell half now, add on a dip
questions.answer: Not yet, wait for day 3 or later
questions.why: Not yet. The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R. We very rarely sell on day 1, and day 3 is about the earliest we'll look. What I want is to sell into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or around 5 to 10R. Big winners pay for all the small stopped losses. Sell too early and you cap the very trades that carry the account.
questions.lesson_line: The first sell is a judgment. Day 3 or later, into a push.

wrong.Yes, sell a third, 3R is the rule: 3R isn't a fixed sell for us. The first sell is a judgment, and rarely this early.
wrong.Yes, sell it all and bank it: That caps the big winners that pay for the losses.
wrong.Sell half now, add on a dip: Adding is never the plan, least of all on a dip. One full buy, one stop.

questions.simple: Not yet. Big winners pay for the small losses, so we let it work and sell into a push from day 3.

reasons: D-013 (the first sell is a judgment, day 3 at the earliest, a 3, 5 or 7 day push); Kullamagi's 3-5 days and 10-20x risk quoted from his page

deeper.counter: Kullamagi sells 1/3 to 1/2 after 3 to 5 days, then moves his stop to breakeven. Same idea as ours: let the first push play out before you sell any.

questions.q: A base pulls back 20%, then 10%, then 5%. Why do those shrinking swings matter?
choices: Fewer sellers are left each time
Volume is rising on each dip
questions.answer: Fewer sellers are left each time
questions.why: Fewer sellers are left each time. The first drop is the big one, when everyone who wants out rushes for the door. The next drop has fewer of them, so it's half as deep. By the 5% swing almost nobody's left to sell. That's why a tightening base is ready. A little buying is enough to push it through the pivot.
questions.lesson_line: Each smaller swing means fewer sellers are left.

wrong.Volume is rising on each dip: It's the other way. Volume dries up as the swings shrink.
wrong.Buyers are losing interest: Smaller dips mean selling is drying up, not buyers leaving.
wrong.It's getting close to the 200-day: The swings say nothing about the 200-day. They show how much selling is left.

questions.simple: Fewer sellers are left each time, so each dip is shallower, and a little buying can push it out.

reasons: Minervini (his 2013 book, on his blog) and ChartMill's guide both give the sellers-scarcer reason, quoted word for word

questions.q: Do you buy it here?
questions.story: A leader is in the first big pullback of a base that might turn into a VCP. It's down 8% from its high and looks cheap.
choices: No, wait for the pivot to trade
Yes, the first dip is cheapest
No, give it two more months
questions.answer: No, wait for the pivot to trade
questions.why: No. Cheap isn't a setup. In the first pullback the supply is still heavy, and you don't know where it stops. There's no tight swing to put a stop under either. Let it build the base. When the last tight swing forms and price trades through its high, that's your buy, with a stop close by.
questions.lesson_line: Don't buy the dip in the middle of the base. Buy the pivot.

wrong.Yes, the first dip is cheapest: Cheap mid-base is a guess. Sellers are still active.
wrong.Yes, but at half size: Smaller size on a guess is still a guess. We buy at the trigger.
wrong.No, give it two more months: Right idea, wrong clock. You wait for the pivot, not a date.

questions.simple: No. Mid-base the sellers are still busy, so you wait for the pivot to trade.

reasons: Minervini's line of least resistance and ChartMill's not during the first pullback, both quoted word for word; the card names buying mid-base as a mistake

questions.q: Ten VCP buys. Seven stop out for -1R each. One makes 8R and two make 2R each. Where does that leave you?
questions.why: +5R. The seven losers cost you 7R. The winners make 8R plus 2R plus 2R, so 12R. 12 minus 7 is +5R. Seven out of ten failed and you still made money. That's the math behind tight stops. Small losses are cheap, and one big winner pays for a pile of them. Take every small loss so you're still around for the 8R.
questions.lesson_line: Lose small and often. One big winner pays for a lot of small losses.

wrong.+12R: That's just the winners. You forgot the seven losses.
wrong.+3R: That misses one of the 2R winners.

questions.simple: Up 5R. The small stopped losses are paid for by a few big winners.

reasons: ChartMill's worked example (its numbers) and Kullamagi's 10-20x quoted word for word; the arithmetic decides whether to accept small losses
